cases.title: Río Blanco Gold Mine, Molleturo: Militarisation and a Court Halt
cases.place: Río Blanco, Molleturo parish, Cuenca canton, Azuay, Ecuador
cases.point: Río Blanco mining project area (EJAtlas coordinates)

lenders.name: Junefield Mineral Resources Holdings (Hong Kong) and Hunan Gold Group (Chinese state-owned), through Ecuagoldmining South America (foreign investors)
lenders.role: Junefield and Hunan Gold's Ecuagoldmining bought the concession rights from Canada's IMC (2012 or 2013, the People's Map gives both), obtained the environmental permit in 2015 and began building the mine in 2016; about US$20.13 million was invested in 2010-2018, according to Ecuador's mining ministry (People's Map of Global China). In 2022 Primicias named Ecuagoldmining's shareholders as two Hong Kong firms, Junefield Gold Investments Limited and Power Fortune Development Limited.

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the mine. The Ecuadorian government listed Río Blanco as one of five strategic mining projects (People's Map of Global China). Junefield Gold Investments filed an arbitration claim against Ecuador under the China-Ecuador investment treaty in October 2022 (Primicias).
cases.community: An August 2017 inspection by Azuay's provincial council recorded the first environmental damage: the Cruz Loma lagoon disappeared after more than 4,000 cubic metres of waste material were dumped in it, and the flow of the Canoas river fell (Expreso). A 2018 FIAN Ecuador report, based on residents' statements and documents, found the mining companies bought property and possession rights inside the concession, some with forged sale titles, splitting the indigenous community's land; many families moved to Cuenca (People's Map of Global China). A Comptroller General review released in July 2019 found environmental and mining agencies had approved the mine without the required water-use authorisations (People's Map of Global China).
cases.suppression: In May 2018, after residents blocked the camps and some protesters set fire to part of the facilities, four people were arrested; on 9 May four indigenous leaders were held for several hours by company employees, who were never tried. The government sent 200 police and 90 soldiers, and 'sabotage' charges were opened against 28 local people (People's Map of Global China). Expreso reported violent clashes between farmers and police that May, with people injured on both sides, and in 2019 found guards and police patrolling the company's new access road in company vehicles.
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources used.
cases.outcome: On 5 June 2018 a Cuenca court ruled that the communities had not been consulted and suspended the project; the provincial court upheld this in August 2018, and the government took the case to the Constitutional Court (People's Map of Global China; Intercontinental Cry). The company cut its payroll from 225 to 24 workers. A local group burned the mining camp during the October 2019 national uprising (EJAtlas). Ecuagoldmining opened a treaty dispute in February 2020, and Junefield filed arbitration in October 2022 (People's Map of Global China; Primicias).

sources.title: Rio Blanco, Molleturo, Azuay, Ecuador
Rio Blanco Mining Project
sources.publisher: The People's Map of Global China (Latinoamérica Sustentable)

sources.title: En la mina de Río Blanco es tiempo de guerra fría
Can the law prevail over Chinese investments in Ecuador?
Minera china demandó a Ecuador por proyecto Río Blanco

cases.confidence_note: The land-purchase findings come from a FIAN Ecuador report summarised by the People's Map. The government and Ecuagoldmining say water contamination has not been shown and that a February 2018 public consultation settled the matter (EJAtlas, citing El Comercio). Primicias names the shareholders as two Hong Kong firms and does not mention Hunan Gold.
cases.ecosystem: The concessions lie in the Molleturo-Mollepungo protective forest, on páramo and water sources bordering Cajas National Park (EJAtlas); the mine entrance is 300 metres from the Llantaguaico lagoon (Expreso).

lvwhy.project: A Hong Kong and Chinese consortium's mine works dried a lagoon and its camps drew protests, arrests and troops.
lvwhy.land: Company purchases of property and possession rights, some on forged titles, split the community's land.

cases.title: San Cristóbal Mine: a Colonial Town Moved for an Open Pit
cases.place: San Cristóbal, Colcha K municipality, Nor Lípez, Potosí, Bolivia

lenders.name: Apex Silver Mines (United States), then Sumitomo Corporation (Japan) (foreign investors)
lenders.role: Apex Silver began drilling in 1996 and set up Minera San Cristóbal in 2000 (Wikipedia). Sumitomo took on the project in 2008 (EJAtlas) and became sole owner in March 2009 (Wikipedia); Apex Silver had sold its company to Sumitomo (Correo del Sur).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the mine. The relocation was set out in a Town Relocation Agreement signed with the company on 9 June 1998 (Wikipedia).

companies.name: Sumitomo Corporation
companies.role: Partner from 2008, sole owner from March 2009 to 2023

cases.community: The town of San Cristóbal, dating from colonial times, sat on the ore body. Under a relocation agreement signed on 9 June 1998, it was moved to a new site inaugurated on 9 June 1999, and its colonial church, a national monument since 1967, was taken down and rebuilt there (Wikipedia; Correo del Sur). The three hills around the old town, held sacred as protectors of the community, are now being mined (EJAtlas). Opponents say the mine pumps close to 50,000 cubic metres of water a day from wells in an area with almost no aquifer recharge, and that the Jaú Kiwa river receives untreated waste (EJAtlas). In April 2010 communities of three provinces blocked roads to the mine, demanding among other things payment for its water use; the company said the water it uses is saline and unfit for people or animals (La Prensa via eju.tv).
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources used.
cases.outcome: The mine operates; it processes about 40,000 tonnes of rock a day and exported US$860 million in 2009 (La Prensa via eju.tv). Bolivia's foreign minister said in 2010 that the mine wastes water without paying the state; the company denied it 'plunders' the country (La Prensa via eju.tv). Sumitomo sold the mine to San Cristobal Mining Inc. in 2023 (Wikipedia).

sources.title: Mina San Cristobal en Potosi y reubicación de la comunidad, Bolivia
San Cristóbal mine (Bolivia)
Minera San Cristóbal dice que no saquea y advierte de paro de actividades
Así es San Cristóbal

cases.confidence_note: The relocation was negotiated and signed with community, municipal and regional authorities; the Wikipedia account follows the company's own description. The water-depletion and pollution complaints come from opponents and the government; the company says the water is saline groundwater.
cases.ecosystem: A dry high plateau at 3,800-4,000 m with 150-200 mm of rain a year; the mine draws on groundwater wells (EJAtlas; eju.tv).

lvwhy.project: A US-founded, later Japanese-owned open-pit mine required the whole town to move.
lvwhy.land: The town site and its sacred hills became the mine.

cases.title: Perenco's Oil Blocks 7 and 21 and the Tribunal's Pollution Finding
cases.place: Blocks 7 and 21, southwest of Puerto Francisco de Orellana (Coca), Orellana and Napo, Ecuador

lenders.name: Perenco (Anglo-French), with Burlington Resources (United States) and earlier OMV (Austria) (foreign investors)
lenders.role: Perenco and OMV took over the blocks in 2001 after Oryx and Kerr-McGee; OMV left in 2004 and Perenco ran the blocks with Burlington until Ecuador ended the contracts on 20 July 2010 (EJAtlas; IISD Investment Treaty News).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the blocks. Perenco sued Ecuador at ICSID, the World Bank Group's arbitration centre; Ecuador counter-claimed for environmental damage (IISD Investment Treaty News).
cases.community: An ICSID tribunal found, in its award of 27 September 2019, that remediating the measured contamination in Blocks 7 and 21 would cost almost US$160 million, of which more than US$93 million was attributable to Perenco's operations, and ordered Perenco to pay Ecuador slightly more than US$54 million after subtracting US$39 million already paid by Burlington (IISD Investment Treaty News). Before Perenco arrived, residents recorded spills, cattle deaths and the death of a person who drank contaminated water at the Gacela field; tests found the school well at Flor de Manduro more contaminated than the rivers (EJAtlas).
cases.killed_note: No death is counted. EJAtlas reports that one person died after drinking contaminated water at the Gacela field during the Oryx period (1990s), before Perenco arrived.
cases.outcome: Ecuador ended the contracts in July 2010 and handed the blocks to state companies Petroecuador and Petroamazonas (IISD Investment Treaty News; EJAtlas). The same 2019 award ordered Ecuador to pay Perenco almost US$449 million for treaty breaches; a separate tribunal awarded Ecuador US$41 million on Burlington's environmental and infrastructure counterclaims (IISD Investment Treaty News).

sources.title: Exploración de petroleo en Bloque 7 y 21, Ecuador
Substantial damages awarded to Perenco for FET breach and expropriation; Ecuador also awarded compensation under environmental counterclaim

cases.confidence_note: The pollution finding comes from an arbitration tribunal. EJAtlas also reports land expropriation and militarisation after spills, apparently under earlier operators, without dates; these are not used here.
cases.ecosystem: Amazon lowland rivers and soils in Orellana; total measured contamination in the two blocks would cost almost US$160 million to clean (IISD Investment Treaty News).

lvwhy.project: A foreign oil consortium's operation left contamination a tribunal valued at over US$93 million.

cases.title: Rucalhue Hydro Dam on the Biobío: Native Forest Cut and a Camp Cleared
cases.place: Rucalhue, between Santa Bárbara and Quilaco, Biobío, Chile

lenders.name: China International Water and Electric Corporation (CWE), subsidiary of China Three Gorges Corporation (Chinese state-owned) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Owner of Rucalhue Energía SpA, which took over the 90 MW project first filed by Brazil's Atiaia Energía (Resumen; EJAtlas).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the project. Its environmental approval was issued in 2016 (EJAtlas).

companies.name: China International Water and Electric Corporation
companies.role: Project owner via Rucalhue Energía SpA

cases.community: Chile's forestry agency CONAF found infractions in two inspections in March 2022: the company had cut native preservation forest containing the vulnerable naranjillo and guindo santo without an approved management plan, and CONAF filed complaints with the local police court of Santa Bárbara (Resumen, citing CONAF). The project's planned works would affect 379 trees of the two species on 8.95 ha (Resumen). Mapuche Pewenche communities and neighbours object that it would be the fourth large dam on the Biobío after Pangue, Ralco and Angostura (EJAtlas).
cases.suppression: A protest camp set up by young residents in early February 2021 was cleared in late July 2021 by a large police contingent; no one was detained because the campers left before police arrived. In early April 2021 the company had filed a criminal complaint against three young people for violent usurpation, threats and robbery, later widened to kidnapping, which residents deny; the court admitted it (Resumen).
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources used.
cases.outcome: Protection appeals by the municipalities of Santa Bárbara and Quilaco were rejected by the Concepción court (EJAtlas). The company asked for the project to be declared of national interest to allow the felling; in 2022 CONAF suspended the request and said work on 11.55 ha of the protected species' habitat was halted pending a ruling on a new indigenous consultation (Resumen).

sources.title: Central Hidroeléctrica Rucalhue, Bíobío, Chile
Gigante hidroeléctrico chino se querelló contra jóvenes movilizados en defensa del río Biobío
Proyecto Central Rucalhue paralizado: Antecedentes podrían decantar en realización de nueva consulta indígena

cases.confidence_note: The illegal felling rests on CONAF statements as reported by Resumen, a regional independent outlet. The company's own account of the protest camp is given only through its court filing.
cases.ecosystem: Native preservation forest with naranjillo and guindo santo on the upper Biobío, already dammed at Pangue, Ralco and Angostura (Resumen; EJAtlas).

lvwhy.project: A Chinese state-owned firm's dam works cut protected native forest and led to court action against protesters.

cases.title: Barrick's Pierina Mine: Police Shootings at Huallapampa and Mareniyoc
cases.place: Pierina mine, Jangas district, Huaraz, Áncash, Peru

lenders.name: Barrick Gold (Canada), through Minera Barrick Misquichilca (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Owner and operator of the Pierina open-pit gold mine, in production from 1998 (EJAtlas; MercoPress).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the mine.
cases.community: On 5 May 2006 community members who worked extracting minerals for the mine gathered at Huallapampa to ask for higher pay and blocked access roads with stones and logs; MercoPress later said the pay dispute was with a service company contracted by Barrick. Police fired tear gas, and in the clash about 20 people were seriously injured, including police (La República via Mines and Communities). In September 2012 villagers of Mareniyoc blocked the mine road from 14 September, demanding the drinking water Barrick had promised after the Shulcan spring and local springs dried up; Barrick said the water supply was outside its control and that residents had refused treated water from the mine (Servindi; MercoPress; BBC via Mines and Communities).
cases.suppression: In 2006, police spokespeople said 30 police officers were employed by the mining company as its security force, and that Barrick sent in a contingent of police; six officers were held by villagers after the clash (La República via Mines and Communities). On 19 September 2012 police tried to clear protesters from the road to the mine (BBC via Mines and Communities); the victim's brother said the shots came from DINOES special operations police sent from Lima. Between four and seven people were injured, including police (MercoPress; Actualidad Ambiental).
cases.killed_note: Two deaths are counted, one in each year, both by police acting for the mine: in 2006 by police that police spokespeople said were employed by the company, and in 2012 by police clearing the mine road. For 5 May 2006, La República named two dead, agronomy student Joel Martel Castromonte, 25, and miner Guillermo Tolentino Abat, 42, while MercoPress and a 2012 Mines and Communities commentary say one person died; only one is counted. The 2012 victim, a villager surnamed Poma aged 54 or 55, is named Nemesio Poma Asnate by Servindi and Demetrio Poma Rosales by RPP (via Actualidad Ambiental) and BBC-based reports.
cases.outcome: Barrick halted the mine after both clashes and resumed operations; in 2012 it said the stoppage was a sign of mourning (MercoPress). Human Rights Watch wrote to Peru's president the next day asking him to stop the use of lethal force against protesters (Mines and Communities). Regional authorities also demanded US$140 million in taxes they said the company owed (EJAtlas).

sources.title: Pierina, Jangas, Perú
Barrick Gold Mining Conflict Leaves Two Dead In Perú
Perú: Comunero de Jangas que exigía agua para su comunidad muere en enfrentamiento
Peruvian villager killed and four injured in clashes over water with Barrick Gold
Deadly clash at Barrick gold mine in Peru (BBC News; Human Rights Watch)
Áncash: un muerto y 7 heridos por enfrentamiento en centro minero Pierina

cases.confidence_note: The 2006 death toll differs between sources (two named by La República, one in MercoPress), and MercoPress says that dispute was with a Barrick contractor, away from the mine. The claim that police were employed by the company comes from police spokespeople quoted by La República. Who fired in 2012 rests on the victim's brother; the victim's name differs between reports. The drying of springs is the community's account; Barrick says the water problem is outside its control.
cases.ecosystem: High Andean slopes of the Cordillera Negra at 4,100 m; villagers say the Shulcan spring and other springs dried up (Servindi).

lvwhy.project: Protests over water and access at a Canadian-owned mine were met with police fire.
lvwhy.labour: The 2006 shooting came during a pay protest by local people working for the mine or its contractor.

cases.title: Tocopilla's Coal Plants and the Saturated-Zone Declaration

lenders.name: Suez-Tractebel / GDF Suez, now Engie (Belgium-France), through Electroandina, and AES Corporation (United States), through AES Gener's Norgener (foreign investors)
lenders.role: Tractebel (Belgium) entered Electroandina, owner of the Tocopilla plant, in 1996 with Iberdrola and Enagás; after it bought them out in 2000, the state copper company Codelco held about 66.7% and Suez-Tractebel 33.3% until GDF Suez bought Codelco's shares in 2010 and the company became E-CL. AES Corporation's subsidiary has held over 90% of AES Gener, owner of Norgener, since 2001 (Wikipedia).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the plants. Chile declared Tocopilla a saturated zone for fine particles in 2007 (DS 50) and imposed a decontamination plan in 2010 (DS 70) with emission caps for each plant (Chile, Ministry General Secretariat of the Presidency).

companies.name: Engie (formerly Suez-Tractebel / GDF Suez)
companies.role: Part-owner of Electroandina from 1996 (33.3% consolidated stake after 2000), owner of E-CL from 2010

companies.name: AES Corporation
companies.role: Controlling owner of AES Gener / Norgener

cases.community: The government's decontamination plan records that of 3,500 tonnes a year of fine particles (PM10) emitted in the zone, 95.2% came from the Electroandina and Norgener power plants, which also emitted 19,395 and 9,971 tonnes of sulphur dioxide a year respectively (DS 70 of 2010). It estimated that meeting the air standard would avoid about 22 deaths during the plan, plus hospital admissions for heart and lung disease (DS 70 of 2010). Residents, including the Chango indigenous people who live from the sea, report respiratory disease, cancer and soot covering roofs, water and the sea (EJAtlas).
cases.killed_note: No death is counted. The 2010 plan estimates about 22 deaths would be avoided by cleaner air; these are statistical projections, not recorded deaths.
cases.outcome: The 2010 plan capped the plants' particle emissions at 2,002 and 1,386 tonnes a year for three years, then 879 and 469 tonnes (DS 70 of 2010). Electroandina became E-CL in 2010 after GDF Suez bought out the state copper company's share (Wikipedia). Tocopilla is listed among Chile's 'sacrifice zones' (EJAtlas).

sources.title: Zona de Sacrificio Tocopilla, Chile
Decreto 70: Establece plan de descontaminación atmosférico para la ciudad de Tocopilla y su zona circundante
sources.publisher: Chile, Ministerio Secretaría General de la Presidencia (Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional)

sources.title: Electroandina
AES Andes

cases.confidence_note: The pollution share and health estimate come from the government's own decree. Chile's state copper company Codelco held the majority of Electroandina (about 66.7%) until 2010, and the Tocopilla plant was built in 1915, long before foreign ownership; Norgener has been over 90% foreign-owned since 2001.
cases.ecosystem: A narrow coastal strip under a cliff where 'coastal fumigation' traps plant emissions over the town and sea (DS 70 of 2010).

lvwhy.project: Coal plants owned in whole or part by foreign firms supplied 95% of the fine particles in a declared saturated zone.
lvwhy.priv: Codelco's Tocopilla plant was partly sold to a Belgian-led group in 1996 and fully to GDF Suez in 2010.

cases.title: Smurfit Kappa's Pine Plantations in Cajibío and the Misak Land Recovery
cases.point: Cajibío town (approximate; plantations lie around it)

lenders.name: Smurfit Kappa Group (Ireland), through Smurfit Kappa Cartón de Colombia (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Majority owner (99% by 2019) of the Colombian paper company, which holds about 3,000 ha of pine and eucalyptus in Cajibío and 70,000 ha nationally (Mongabay; EJAtlas).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the plantations. They hold Forest Stewardship Council certification (Mongabay).
cases.community: In Cajibío, 110 Misak families next to the plantations farm one or two hectares each, below the 4-6 ha the state sets as the minimum for a farm family; Mongabay verified three cases of trees planted next to streams, against the legal 30-metre buffer, and residents report wells running low, though no groundwater study has been done (Mongabay). In 2017 the Land Restitution Court of Cali ordered the company to return 78 ha to the Rivera family in another department, finding it had profited from the armed conflict by buying the land cheaply (Mongabay).
cases.suppression: On 2 August 2021, during a police operation to evict indigenous and farming families occupying Smurfit Kappa timber land at the El Retiro farm, vereda El Arado, Huber Samir Camayo Fajardo, 23, was shot in the back and died in hospital in Popayán; witnesses blamed the ESMAD riot police, and the Inspector General's office (Procuraduría) opened a preliminary inquiry into police officers (Infobae; El Tiempo). His death set off a riot in which Cajibío's town hall was burned (Radio Nacional). Locals also said company workers attacked them during the 2021 protests and one person was arrested by armed forces while driving home (Mongabay).
cases.killed_note: One death is counted: Huber Samir Camayo Fajardo, shot on 2 August 2021 during a police eviction from the company's land; the Procuraduría is investigating police officers. Not counted: Juvencio Cerquera, killed on 9 November 2022 in Sotará by a bullet Mongabay says was allegedly fired by a company worker; no second source was found.
cases.outcome: From July 2021 indigenous people and farmers occupied the plantations and cleared about 1,000 ha of pine and eucalyptus to plant food crops; further uprooting followed in May 2022 (Mongabay). The company denies land grabbing and says it carries out rigorous legal checks before buying land (Mongabay).

sources.title: Misak and farmers struggle against Smurfit Kappa Colombia (SKC) in Cajibio, Cauca, Colombia
FSC-certified paper plantation faces farmer backlash in Colombia
Procuraduría indaga muerte de Huber Samir Camayo, habitante de Cajibío, Cauca
Cauca: Investigan muerte de joven por disparo en confrontaciones
Indagación preliminar a la Policía por muerte de un campesino en Cajibío, Cauca
Colombia: la lucha de los misak contra una papelera multinacional para recuperar su territorio ancestral
Huber Samir Camayo (attack record)

cases.confidence_note: The killing during the eviction is reported by national press and is under investigation by the Procuraduría; police said the prosecutor's office would establish what happened. Land-grab claims in Cajibío are the Misak's and farmers' account, which the company denies; the only court ruling on land concerns a different department. Water depletion has not been measured.
cases.ecosystem: Andean farmland converted to patula pine and eucalyptus monocultures; trees planted within the 30-metre buffer of streams (Mongabay).

lvwhy.land: An Irish-owned paper company's plantations hold land the Misak and farmers say was taken from them.
lvwhy.project: Police evicted occupiers from the company's plantations, and a young man was shot dead.

cases.title: Nova Atlântida Resort Plan and the Tremembé of Itapipoca
cases.place: São José and Buriti villages, Tremembé da Barra do Mundaú, Itapipoca, Ceará, Brazil

lenders.name: Grupo Afirma / Nova Atlântida (Spain) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Spanish group led by Juan Ripoll Mari planning a 3,100 ha resort city with 27 hotels and three golf courses on 12 km of coast, budgeted at US$15 billion in the Ceará press (Agência Pública).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the project. Ceará's environment council (Coema) approved its impact study on 3 November 2004 and the state agency licensed it; the same day the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office filed for the licence to be suspended (Agência Pública).
cases.community: Tremembé leaders say that when the company arrived in 2002 it showed a map of their land divided among group companies, told them they would be removed, and fenced areas at São José and Buriti do Meio (Agência Pública). Agência Pública reports that a part of São José near the beach was held by Nova Atlântida with guards for 11 years until the Tremembé took it back in 2013; in September 2014 their huts, crops and a cart there were burned at night by people the Tremembé say were linked to the company (Agência Pública). Land and sea access were gradually restricted, limiting fishing and farming (EJAtlas). The community split after some members were paid to side with the company, according to the leaders (Agência Pública). A study for prosecutors found the impact study had left out indigenous presence and five archaeological sites; the head of the consultancy that wrote it was later convicted over fraudulent studies for other projects in Ceará (Agência Pública).
cases.suppression: EJAtlas reports that Military Police and company employees threatened and physically abused some opponents of the project, without dates.
cases.killed_note: No death is counted. Tremembé leader Erbene says a young indigenous woman was stoned to death in a vehicle amid the prejudice stirred by the dispute (Agência Pública); the sources do not tie this to the company.
cases.outcome: Funai published its study recognising the Tremembé land on 6 February 2012 (Agência Pública). The Justice Minister declared it Tremembé land in 2015, and a federal court archived the project in 2016 (EJAtlas).

sources.title: “Cidade Nova Atlântida” mega-tourist-complex threatens the Tremembé indigenous people, Ceará, Brazil
No Ceará, terra dos Tremembé é ameaçada por resort espanhol

cases.confidence_note: The fencing, guards, payments and the burning of huts are the Tremembé's account to Agência Pública; the company could not be reached by Agência Pública. The company and local politicians said there were no indigenous people in the area, and the company showed a land title bought from a local couple (Agência Pública; EJAtlas).
cases.ecosystem: Coastal dunes, lagoons, springs, mangroves and forest at Praia da Baleia (Agência Pública).

lvwhy.land: A Spanish developer fenced and claimed indigenous coastal land for a resort city.

cases.title: Delta & Pine's Pesticide-Treated Seed Dump at Rincón-í

lenders.name: Delta & Pine Land (United States), through Delta & Pine Paraguay (foreign investor)
lenders.role: The US cottonseed company's Paraguayan subsidiary, Deltapine Paraguay, Inc., imported the seed and dumped the expired stock (PAN North America; GRAIN; Delta and Pine Land 1999 annual report). A planned takeover by Monsanto was under way in 1999 (PAN North America).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the company. Paraguay's agriculture ministry had authorised the import of 84,000 sacks of Delta & Pine cottonseed in 1997 (GRAIN, from IUF).
cases.community: From 27 November 1998, over about ten days, 30,000 sacks (about 660 tonnes) of expired cottonseed treated with the organophosphate pesticides acephate and chlorpyrifos were dumped over 1.5 ha and covered with a thin layer of soil, less than 170 metres from a primary school with 262 pupils, in a community of about 3,000 people (PAN North America; GRAIN). Vertigo, nausea, headaches, memory loss and skin rashes appeared at once and worsened after rain; clinical tests on 70 residents by a Paraguayan consultancy found more than half showed signs of poisoning (PAN North America; GRAIN).
cases.killed_note: No death is counted. The IUF food workers' federation reported that a local man, Mr Ruiz, 30, a father of five, died on 28 December 1998 and that his official death certificate gives 'acute poisoning' from the Delta & Pine Land seed (PAN North America, from an IUF press release); EJAtlas names him Agustín Ruiz Aranda. No source independent of the IUF account was found.
cases.outcome: The health and agriculture ministries acknowledged the test results but did not act at first (PAN North America). In July 2004 a court in Paraguarí convicted the landowner and a Delta & Pine official, with sentences of two years and 15 months and a fine; the company's representative in Paraguay left the country (EJAtlas).

sources.title: Delta & Pine's toxic waste in Paraguay
Pesticide Disaster in Paraguay (PANUPS)
Paraguay: semillas de la muerte (IUF/UITA denuncia)
Delta and Pine Land Company, Form 10-K for fiscal 1999 (subsidiaries list)

cases.confidence_note: The poisoning and clinical tests are reported by the IUF food workers' federation (through PAN and GRAIN), which campaigned for the victims; the 2004 conviction is reported by EJAtlas only. The company's own filings confirm the Paraguayan subsidiary.
cases.ecosystem: About 1.5 ha of farmland received over 4,000 kg of pesticides in the seed coating, according to a US consultancy cited by the IUF (GRAIN).

lvwhy.project: A US seed firm's subsidiary dumped pesticide-coated seed beside a village school.

cases.title: Gran Colombia Gold and the 2017 Miners' Strike in Segovia and Remedios
cases.place: Segovia and Remedios, northeast Antioquia, Colombia
cases.point: Segovia town (the EJAtlas point sat about 17 km north of the town)

lenders.name: Gran Colombia Gold (Canada), after merging with Medoro Resources (Canada) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Took over the Frontino Gold Mines titles in Segovia in 2010 after Frontino's liquidation (EJAtlas); in 2017 it demanded that local miners stop working on land it claims (Colombia Reports).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the company. The 2017 strike was also against government decrees the miners said pushed small and medium miners into illegality (Colombia Reports).

companies.name: Gran Colombia Gold
companies.role: Title holder of the Segovia mines

cases.community: About 7,000 local miners struck from 21 July 2017 against Gran Colombia Gold and government decrees (Colombia Reports). By mid-August Segovia's mayor said families were going hungry, students had no classes and commerce was paralysed (Semana). A verification mission with the Inspector General's office found the municipal hospital short of medicines and the ESMAD riot police within 100 metres of it (Colombia Reports). The towns' economy depends almost wholly on mining, about 95% according to the national miners' confederation (Colombia Reports).
cases.suppression: Clashes with the ESMAD riot police injured 12 people on 31 July; the governor sent in the army and imposed a curfew (Colombia Reports). Police said 19 people were captured, most held on terrorism and weapons charges, and 9 minors detained (Semana). A rights commission accompanied by the Inspector General's office reported excessive force, snipers and tear gas fired into homes, schools and hospitals (Colombia Reports).
cases.killed_note: No death is counted, as the sources do not establish who caused them. Three people died during the strike (Colombia Reports), including a 17-year-old killed by two men on a motorcycle on 3 August and 18-year-old Brandon Estiv Ochoa Estrada on 15 August; miners said police shot him, police said he was hit by shrapnel (Colombia Reports; Semana).
cases.outcome: Seventeen meetings among the miners, the governor's office and Gran Colombia Gold had produced no agreement by mid-August 2017 (Semana). Armed groups have long fought over the area's gold, and EJAtlas reports continued killings of small miners.

cases.title: Vale's La Morada Exploration and the Armed Guards of Cerro Mogol
cases.place: Cerro Mogol, between Jesús, Pedro Gálvez and Cachachi districts, Cajamarca, Peru

lenders.name: Vale (Companhia Vale do Rio Doce, Brazil), through Minera Miski Mayo (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Vale's Peruvian subsidiary explored a 13,000 ha concession for copper, gold and manganese at La Morada from about 2004 (La República via OCMAL; EJAtlas).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the project. The exploration ran on a sworn statement rather than a full environmental study (EJAtlas).
cases.community: La República found that Miski Mayo formed armed 'defence squads', hiring people with criminal records; at a 21 May 2007 meeting on Cerro Mogol called by the regional government, up to 30 firearms were counted among the company's bodyguards and allied ronderos, and the company's 30 site guards were issued shotguns and balaclavas (La República via OCMAL). Most of the 15 communities in the Condebamba valley opposed the project, citing water used for dairy farming (La República via Business & Human Rights Resource Centre; OCMAL).
cases.suppression: Opponents reported house raids, physical attacks, kidnapping attempts and death threats (La República via OCMAL). After a September 2007 strike the company filed charges against the president of the river-basin defence front and 9 others, who were sentenced in 2009 to four years in prison and a fine; the Cajamarca High Court later annulled the sentence (EJAtlas).
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources used.
cases.outcome: Exploration was halted in August 2007 and the project was stopped by 2009 (Business & Human Rights Resource Centre; EJAtlas). Canada's Teck acquired the concessions in 2018 (EJAtlas).

cases.title: B2Gold's La Libertad Expansion and the 2013 Santo Domingo Eviction
cases.point: Santo Domingo and La Libertad mining area (EJAtlas coordinates)

lenders.name: B2Gold (Canada), through Desarrollo Minero de Nicaragua (DESMINIC) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Acquired 100% of the La Libertad open-pit gold mine in 2009 and found the Jabalí vein south of Santo Domingo in 2010 (EJAtlas); B2Gold and DESMINIC's arrival in Chontales led to the protests (Legal Cultures of the Subsoil).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the mine. Nicaragua's government had promoted mining investment since 2001 (EJAtlas).
cases.community: Residents said the mine's operation contaminated water sources and damaged aquifers, and threatened the work of about 3,600 people in small-scale mining in Santo Domingo (Legal Cultures of the Subsoil), a mining town since 1870 (EJAtlas). EJAtlas reports a hill cleared of forest without an impact study and high pollutant levels in the Mico river.
cases.suppression: On 9 February 2013, after a 105-day protest, about 200 riot police evicted the camp and detained more than 50 representatives of the El Cafetal and Santo Domingo miners' groups; about 141 people were reported injured by police. Twelve leaders were taken to the Managua jail known as El Chipote and kept in pre-trial detention on charges including threats, injuries, obstruction of officials and usurpation of private property until their release in April 2013 (Legal Cultures of the Subsoil). Nicaragua's human rights centre CENIDH called the use of force disproportionate, arbitrary and illegitimate (Legal Cultures of the Subsoil).
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources used.
cases.outcome: B2Gold obtained permission to mine the Jabalí vein (EJAtlas). In 2014 some residents filed a civil action over injuries from the 9 February police operation (Legal Cultures of the Subsoil).

cases.ecosystem: Forested hills and the Mico river, which drains toward Bluefields on the Caribbean coast (EJAtlas).

cases.title: Rafey Landfill Concession and the Santiago Waste Pickers
cases.place: Rafey landfill, Cienfuegos district, Santiago de los Caballeros, Dominican Republic

lenders.name: Green Wheels Dominicana (United States origin) and Lavo Investments (Italy) (foreign investors)
lenders.role: Green Wheels, described as of US origin, won the city's international tender for waste management and energy production on 4 July 2011 (Noticia.do); the Italian firm Lavo ran recycling at the site from 2014 (Diario Libre), and from 2017 Cilpen Global, described by the pickers' association as the former Lavo Investment, took over (International Alliance of Waste Pickers).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the concession. The city awarded it by international public tender (Noticia.do). An earlier recycling centre for the waste pickers had been funded by Galician (Spanish regional) development aid (EJAtlas).

companies.name: Green Wheels Dominicana
companies.hq: Santiago de los Caballeros, Dominican Republic

cases.community: On 2 June 2014 more than 350 waste pickers stopped work and blocked garbage trucks, saying the Italian company Lavo had not paid them for almost a month; the park's director said payment would follow (Diario Libre). After fires at the landfill in late June and early July 2017, the city removed the pickers from the landfill and barred them from entering while Cilpen Global installed automated sorting; the pickers' association said 426 recyclers were being pushed out and asked for compensation and jobs with the company (International Alliance of Waste Pickers). The association had asked Green Wheels for RD$40 million to leave the landfill (Noticia.do).
cases.suppression: Santiago's mayor called the 2017 fires an act of terrorism, asked for the landfill to be militarised, said action had begun with the National Police, and said 90% of the pickers were undocumented Haitians (Diario Digital RD). Police arrested the association's president, Juan Rosario, at home, accusing him of the fires and of carrying illegal weapons; the association called it a plot to expel the pickers (International Alliance of Waste Pickers).
cases.killed_note: No death is counted. EJAtlas alone reports clashes with armed private guards in late 2014 that injured 18 pickers and a picker shot dead by private security shortly after; no second source was found.
cases.outcome: From 2017 recycling at the site was run by Cilpen Global (Diario Digital RD; International Alliance of Waste Pickers). The city said it had identified who set the fires but had not named them (Noticia.do).

cases.title: Curipamba-El Domo Copper-Gold Project, Las Naves: Police Crackdowns and Prison Sentences
cases.place: Las Naves canton, Bolívar province, Ecuador

lenders.name: Salazar Resources, Adventus Mining and Silvercorp Metals (Canada), through Curimining S.A. (foreign investors)
lenders.role: Curimining holds the concession; by 2025 it was a joint venture of Silvercorp Metals (75%) and Salazar Resources (25%), after Adventus Mining's period as partner (Business & Human Rights Resource Centre; Prensa Latina).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the project.
cases.community: Farmers of Jerusalén, El Triunfo, Salinas and neighbouring communities fear contamination of the water sources near the project; Acción Ecológica says Curimining has worked there since 2006 without proper environmental consultation (EJAtlas; Prensa Latina). In June 2025 residents blocked the entry of mining machinery and denounced the environmental consultation for El Domo as fraudulent (Business & Human Rights Resource Centre).
cases.suppression: In 2007 the prosecutor of Echeandía opened proceedings against about 30 community members after protesters destroyed drill cores, and in 2010 police repressed a protest and set up a camp 300 metres from the works (EJAtlas). In March 2024 six local defenders were sentenced to three years in prison and a fine of ten basic salaries for alleged illicit association, in a case Prensa Latina ties to Curimining (Prensa Latina). On 24 June 2025 national police repressed residents who had been blocking mining machinery for more than a month; people were reported injured, including a minor (Business & Human Rights Resource Centre, relaying CONAIE, the National Anti-Mining Front and Acción Ecológica).
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources used.
cases.outcome: Curimining, Salazar Resources and Silvercorp did not respond to the Business & Human Rights Resource Centre's request for comment on the June 2025 crackdown. Indigenous federation CONAIE said President Daniel Noboa's family group has been a shareholder in Adventus Mining since 2019 (Prensa Latina).

cases.title: La Zanja Exploration Camp and the November 2004 Pulán Protest
cases.place: La Zanja, Pulán district, Santa Cruz province, Cajamarca, Peru

lenders.name: Newmont Mining (United States), 47% owner with Peru's Buenaventura (53%) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Part-owner of the La Zanja gold and silver exploration project (Associated Press via Mines and Communities; EJAtlas).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the project.
cases.community: Farmers feared mining at the head of the watershed would contaminate water used for health and farming (Weekly News Update on the Americas; EJAtlas). On 16 November 2004 about 2,000 farmers, many of them rondas members, took over the camp and burned buildings and vehicles as 200 workers fled; a 48-hour civic strike followed in Santa Cruz province, with 5,000 marching in Pulán (Weekly News Update on the Americas, from La República).
cases.suppression: Police used tear gas but could not regain control at first; they retook the camp on 17 November and arrested 18 people, who were released the same day after appearing before a judge; the judge ordered the arrest of 23 more, including the mayor of Tongod; 200 more riot police were sent from Chiclayo to defend the camp (Weekly News Update on the Americas, from La República). The Associated Press reported 12 arrests and three people slightly injured.
cases.killed_note: No death is counted, as accounts of who fired differ. Farmer Juan Montenegro Lingán, 53, was shot dead; the prosecutor said a local resident fired as the protest spilled onto his land, while the provincial governor had said a mine worker shot him (Associated Press via Mines and Communities; Weekly News Update on the Americas).
cases.outcome: Buenaventura said it would not yield to pressure and would continue exploring (Weekly News Update on the Americas); EJAtlas reports the company temporarily left and later reopened the project, which went into production.

cases.title: Mejillones Bay: Coal Plants, Spills and an Oxygen-Starved Seabed

lenders.name: Engie (France) and AES Corporation (United States), through AES Gener (foreign investors)
lenders.role: Engie runs the CTM1 and CTM2 coal plants and AES Gener the Cochrane and Angamos plants in Mejillones (El Mostrador, citing the national human rights institute's conflict map); AES Corporation holds over 90% of AES Gener (Wikipedia).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the plants.

companies.name: Engie
companies.role: Owner of CTM1 and CTM2 plants

companies.name: AES Corporation
companies.role: Controlling owner of AES Gener (Angamos, Cochrane)

cases.community: In February 2020 six tonnes of coal bound for AES Gener spilled into the bay during loading by a port operator's worker, after more than ten similar spills in two years at the same port (El Mostrador). A Ministry of Environment study released in 2019 confirmed accumulation of hazardous substances and oxygen depletion (anoxia) on the bay floor, according to Terram researcher Hernán Ramírez (El Mostrador). In January 2024 the Antofagasta environmental evaluation commission found a substantial change in the residual free chlorine in the cooling-water discharge of AES Gener's Angamos plant and partly modified its permit (Reporte Minero). A 2018 oil spill hit Dos Quebradas beach (El Mostrador). Residents report respiratory and other illness from the industrial park (EJAtlas).
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources used.
cases.outcome: The municipality filed a complaint with the Environment Superintendency, which gave the port company 72 hours to report and 15 working days to present monitoring results (El Mostrador). The Committee of Ministers rejected appeals over the Angamos permit in January 2026 but added monitoring and water-quality studies; residents have taken the case to the Environmental Tribunal, and the authority cites the plant's commitment to close its coal units early (Reporte Minero).

The one official finding tied to a foreign-owned plant is the Angamos chlorine discharge change. Health complaints rest on EJAtlas.
cases.ecosystem: Mejillones bay, whose seabed shows accumulated hazardous substances and low oxygen (El Mostrador, citing a Ministry of Environment study).
